One of the harder things we had to figure out was multi-cultural, networked, community governance. It took many experiments. 
We had to solve for: 
● Speed 
● Wisdom 
● The value of experience 
● Effectiveness 
● Right relationships 
Each community and the many jurisdictions had to find ways to make consequential decisions. 
One key was finding networked/linked governance models that cultivated insight. We use a hybrid of the Iroquois two-vote process with 100 ‘’representatives’’ who choose & can take away leadership from 3-person leader formations. 
We are still working on the best means to coordinate globally - but we’ve come a long way. 
Another key wasn’t about structure or process - it was re-building shared community relationships and trust.

Another key wasn’t about structure or process - it was re-building shared community relationships and trust. 
People also knew what was real and fact and what was not. Debates and disagreements still happened, of course, but no one debated facts. And we just had much better sense-making ways. 
Some of the early experiments and some of the consequential decisions ‘’slowed innovation’’ - intentionally and unintentionally breaking exponential capitalistic growth cycles. We tried out and found value in making sure governance holds the perspective of each living generation. 
This design worked because we had to move through many decisions - actual decisions that cut through fragmentation, polarization - we had to move faster than Big Tech & in service to the Earth. 
People felt seen and part of governance, as we not only met the basic needs of people (food, shelter, services) but proactively leaned into connection with each other. 
Governance today is primarily local – we often say ‘’hyper-local’’ - with annual gatherings among communities to share discoveries, meals, and to enjoy each other’s company - even with something called ‘’dating’’. 
In governance and in day-to-day life we are not afraid of wise friction – spurred by differences of understanding and life experiences. We have and practice a deeper understanding of our own minds - and of the nature of contentment. We figured out that contentment is not continuous dopamine hits - but rather a way of being.

There were, and still are disagreements about government and governance. Some practice a world in which all forms of government are abolished. There is no government, only people in relationship, making decisions to care for one another. Others believe that the role of government is truly public servants where institutions exist to facilitate collective care and joy, not control. They manage urban planning, resources, conflict resolution, and community care. They answer to the people and are measured on the happiness and well-being of their community. People are able to play an active role in their government and feel empowered to speak their mind and make their voices heard rather than exist passively.

Whatever one’s preference is, decisions are no longer made by corrupt politicians beholden to the few, but by those most impacted by the problems that still exist, for the greater good. Power is a personal feeling rather than a status of control.
